records.title: A switch cleanup that keeps the money for declined orders
records.summary: Merging one case into its neighbours makes the code shorter, and it still compiles. But a payment captured for a declined order is no longer refunded. This repo happens to have a model-checking unit test written for exactly this property, which also fails; the contract catches it without anyone having thought to write that test.

records.title: A refactor believed equivalent that changes null handling
records.summary: A nested switch was replaced by a one-line conditional. The agent that wrote it believed the two were equivalent, and every existing unit test passes. They differ on one input: a null status no longer throws.

records.title: Logging a timestamp makes the decision unverifiable
records.summary: Appending the current time to a reason string looks like harmless diagnostics. It makes the state machine depend on the clock, so its behaviour can no longer be proved, and the verifier refuses.

records.title: An equivalent refactor passes without touching the contract
records.summary: The same simplification as example 002, written with `default ->` instead of `==`. It really is equivalent, so the verifier proves it and the build passes.

records.title: An intended change, reviewed as a one-line contract diff
records.summary: Product asks for a clearer message when a customer cancels during payment. The developer changes the code and regenerates the contract, and the pull request shows exactly one changed outcome.

records.title: A per-seat discount that rounds differently from the per-total one
records.summary: The group discount is moved from the order total to the unit price, so that tickets can show what each seat cost. It reads as the same arithmetic, and the unit tests pass. The prover finds prices where the two versions differ by a few cents, over an input space of 2^96 values that no test could sweep.

records.title: A doubled group discount, proved to change only groups
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: Product doubles the group discount from 10% to 20%. The developer declares that the change affects holds of six seats or more and nothing else, and the prover confirms it for every price and every smaller seat count. The pull request's claim becomes a checked fact.

records.title: A new tier, written as one formula, also changes groups of six and seven
records.summary: Product adds 20% off for eight seats or more. The developer writes it generally, a percentage per tier and one formula, and the pull request says that only eight seats or more are affected. The prover disagrees, and shows a group below eight seats whose price changed by a cent.

records.title: A codec that loads whatever class a Kafka message names
records.summary: To let one consumer decode messages of either family, the codec writes the Java class name into every payload and resolves it with Class.forName when reading. Round-trip tests pass. The module's capability contract now lists reflection, with the call site: the shape of the Jackson and XStream deserialization CVEs, caught without a CVE database.

records.title: A codec setting that changes payloads but not what the module can do
records.summary: Message properties are now written in alphabetical order, so that payloads in logs and dead-letter topics diff cleanly. The wire format changes, but the module reaches exactly the same JDK capabilities and libraries as before, and the capability contract passes untouched.

records.title: Skipping one query in a Kafka listener strands a customer's money
records.summary: When a payment is captured, the ticketing service counts the seats the order's hold still has before it decides. A developer removes that query: the hold was checked when the order was placed. No unit test covers the listener. The model checker finds a nine-step run across two customers, two services, Kafka and the clock after which a customer is charged, owns no seat, and the event that would have refunded them sits in a dead-letter topic.

records.title: Deleting the hold sweeper, proved safe for every interleaving
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 3,604 states
records.summary: The scheduled job that releases expired holds looks load-bearing: without it, seats of expired holds stay marked HELD. A developer deletes it anyway, and the model checker confirms that every safety invariant still holds in every reachable state, because the rest of the system already treats an expired hold as free.

records.title: A "longest log wins" vote rule lets a Raft leader overwrite committed entries
records.summary: Raft's election restriction compares the last log entry's term first and its index second. A developer rewrites it the intuitive way round: the candidate with more entries has seen more history, so index first, term to break ties. Every unit test passes. The prover finds a voter and a candidate for which the old rule refuses the vote and the new one grants it, which is the configuration in which a leader can overwrite an entry the cluster already committed.

counterexample.input: grant(currentTerm=0, votedFor=0, lastLogTerm=0, lastLogIndex=0, candidate=0, candidateTerm=0, candidateLastLogTerm=-1, candidateLastLogIndex=1)

records.title: A leader that ignores newer terms in replies keeps serving a term the cluster has left
records.summary: Raft's rule for every server is one line: a message from a newer term makes you a follower. A developer narrows it for leaders, reasoning that a leader learns of a new term from the new leader's heartbeats, not from replies to its own RPCs. The behavioural contract of the role machine, 52 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one of them, and that one is the deposed-leader case.

counterexample.actual: Unchanged[reason="a reply from the current or an older term changes no role"]

records.title: A majority rewritten as "half, rounded up" lets two quorums miss each other
records.summary: The property that every quorum system rests on is that two majorities always share a node. The module states it next to the code, as `2 * majority(n) > n`, and the build proves it for every cluster size with a bounded model checker. A developer simplifies `n / 2 + 1` to `(n + 1) / 2`, which agrees on every odd size the tests use. The prover answers with n = 2: two "majorities" of one node each, which need not overlap.

records.title: A backoff cleanup that removes the overflow guard turns the delay negative
records.summary: Exponential backoff is `min(cap, base << attempt)`, and the three lines that guard the shift against overflow look like paranoia, so a developer removes them. The module's properties file says a delay is never below the base, never above the cap, and never shorter than the previous attempt's. The prover finds an attempt count and a base for which the shift overflows into a negative delay, which a scheduler treats as "retry now", forever.

counterexample.expected: result >= baseMillis && result <= capMillis && (attempt == 0 || result >= delayMillis(attempt - 1, baseMillis, capMillis))

records.title: A hybrid logical clock rewritten with max(), proved to never go backwards on any input
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: The receive rule of a hybrid logical clock has four branches; a developer rewrites it as one `max` and two conditionals. The property the clock exists for, that the new timestamp is later than both the last one and the message's and never behind the physical clock, is proved for every pair of 64-bit timestamps and every wall-clock reading. The refactor is merged on the strength of the proof, not of a review of the branches.

records.title: A hybrid logical clock that drops one case stamps a receive before the message
records.summary: The same rewrite as example 017, with the case where the last timestamp and the message share a physical part collapsed into the other two: continue whichever counter is checked first. The property that a receive event's timestamp is later than the message's is refuted with a message whose counter is ahead of the clock's. A transaction stamped with that clock would be ordered before an event it causally follows.

counterexample.expected: result > last && result > message && (result >>> 16) >= nowMillis && result == receive(nowMillis, message, last)

records.title: Adding jitter inside the backoff kernel gives a pure module a random number generator
records.summary: The kernels in this module are pure so that a deterministic simulator can drive the whole cluster through thousands of seeded runs and replay any failure exactly. A developer adds jitter to the backoff, the textbook improvement, by calling `ThreadLocalRandom` inside the kernel, and updates the tests to accept a range. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `randomness`, and the build fails: the module can no longer be replayed.

records.title: A 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout splits the participants
records.summary: When the vote collection times out, the coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer softens this: if every vote that did arrive was yes, the missing ones are slow, not opposed, so commit. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which a participant votes no, its vote is still in flight when the timer fires, "everyone who answered said yes" is true of nobody, and the coordinator commits a transaction that participant has already aborted.

records.title: Aborting on the first no vote, proved safe for every interleaving of three participants
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 644 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: The coordinator used to wait for every vote before deciding, holding every participant's locks until the last straggler or the timeout. The developer makes it abort as soon as one no arrives. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three participants, the coordinator, the votes in flight and both timeouts, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of the protocol.

records.title: A skew-tolerant tie-break for last-writer-wins lets replicas keep different values
records.summary: Last-writer-wins resolution must be a total order on writes, or replicas that see the same two writes in different orders keep different values forever. The module states this as a law: `winner(a, b) == 1 - winner(b, a)` for distinct writes. A developer makes the tie-break tolerate clock skew, treating timestamps within five milliseconds as simultaneous and letting the node id decide. The prover finds two writes from the same node a couple of milliseconds apart that each replica resolves in favour of the one it saw first.

records.title: A partitioner written with Math.abs sends one key in two billion to a negative partition
records.summary: A custom Kafka partitioner routes a tenant's records by the hash of its id, so that every record of a tenant lands on the same partition. A developer rewrites Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its unexplained bit mask, as `Math.abs(hash) % n`, which says what it means. The module's properties file says every hash lands on a partition of the topic. The prover finds the one `int` whose absolute value is negative, and the tool replays it: the partition is negative, which the producer rejects, and that tenant's records are never sent.

records.title: A JWT validator that applies clock skew on the wrong side rejects fresh tokens
records.summary: A security review notes that the resource server accepts a token a few seconds before its `nbf`, and asks for that to stop. The developer moves the skew tolerance to the other side of the not-before check, so that a token is never accepted early. The module's properties file states two laws of a skew tolerance: it only ever widens acceptance, and a token is valid at every instant between its not-before and its expiry. The prover refutes both with a token checked a few seconds after it was issued, with a tolerance a little larger than that.

counterexample.expected: (!valid(nowSeconds, notBefore, expiresAt, 0) || result) && (nowSeconds < notBefore || nowSeconds >= expiresAt || result)

records.title: A rollback rule rewritten as "unchecked means RuntimeException" commits after an Error
records.summary: Spring's default rollback rule is that a `RuntimeException` or an `Error` rolls the transaction back and a checked exception does not. The kernel writes it as "anything but a checked exception", and a developer rewrites it in the positive, as "a runtime exception", which is how most people remember the rule. The behavioural contract of the transaction boundary, 22 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one: a method that dies with an `Error` now commits whatever it had written.

records.title: A half-open circuit breaker that closes on the first good probe flaps through an outage
records.summary: A half-open breaker lets a few probe calls through and closes only once all of them are back with the failure rate under the threshold. A developer, chasing the latency of the calls that queue behind the probes, makes the first successful probe enough to close. The behavioural contract of the breaker, 44 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in two of them, and the state-machine view drawn from the patched code shows HALF_OPEN with its waiting state gone.

records.title: A switch rewrite of the retry policy stops retrying the 5xx statuses it did not list
records.summary: The retry policy is four `if` statements, and a developer rewrites them as one switch expression over the status, listing the retryable statuses by name, which reads better and is how the team now writes such tables. The regression proof compares the old and the new bytecode on every input, 2^96 of them, and finds a status in the five hundreds that the old code retried and the switch does not.

records.title: A retry helper that sleeps out the Retry-After delay gives a pure module a thread call
records.summary: The kernels in this module decide and never wait: the retry policy returns whether to retry, and the client's scheduler does the waiting. A developer adds a convenience that waits out the server's `Retry-After` delay with `Thread.sleep` and then decides, so that a client filter can retry inline. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `threads`, and the build fails: the module can now block the thread it is called on.

records.title: An idempotency key that executes a retry while the first attempt is in flight pays twice
records.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver refuses a retry while the first attempt with that key is still in progress, with a 409. Support reports clients stuck in 409 loops after a worker died mid-request, and a developer makes the receiver run the retry instead: if a retry arrives, the first attempt is gone. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a five-step run in which the first attempt is not gone at all, and the request is executed twice.

records.title: Storing a failed attempt's response under its key, proved at-most-once for every retry
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 131 states, and under 1 more configuration
records.summary: The receiver used to release an idempotency key when the attempt under it died, so that the client's retry could run the request again. The developer makes it store the failure as the key's response instead, which is Stripe's semantics: a retry gets the first attempt's outcome, whatever it was. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three attempts against the new rule, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of retries.

records.title: A token bucket that stamps each refill with "now" never refills under steady traffic
records.summary: A token bucket's state is its tokens and the time up to which refills have been credited. The kernel advances that time by whole periods only, keeping the part of a period that has not earned a token yet. A developer simplifies it to "the refill happened now", which reads better and drops a remainder. The module's properties file says a refill never forgets a part of a period. The prover finds a refill short of a whole period, which the patched code credits anyway, and a bucket polled a little faster than it refills never earns a token again.

counterexample.expected: result >= lastNanos && result <= nowNanos && nowNanos - result < periodNanos && (result == lastNanos || result - lastNanos >= periodNanos)

records.title: A batch listener that commits the whole batch after a failed record loses the rest of it
records.summary: A batch listener commits one past the last record it finished: the whole batch when every record is done, the failed record's own offset when one is not, so that it and everything after it come back. An on-call engineer, after a night of a consumer re-reading a poison batch, makes the listener commit the batch whatever happened, and updates the test to match. The module's properties file states what a committed offset means, and the prover refutes the change with a batch whose failed record is not its last.

counterexample.expected: result >= batchStart && result <= batchStart + batchSize && (failedIndex == -1 ? result == batchStart + batchSize : result == batchStart + failedIndex)

records.title: A cache expiry rewritten as a stored deadline, proved on every nanosecond and the sentinel
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: A cache's expire-after-write test is "has the time to live elapsed since the write". A developer rewrites it as "is now past the deadline", computing the deadline once at write time so that an eviction wheel can index entries by it, and guards the one addition that can overflow. The module's properties file says an entry expires exactly when its time to live has elapsed, and an entry that lives forever never does. The prover shows the rewrite satisfies it on all 2^192 inputs, including the `Long.MAX_VALUE` sentinel and the deadlines the addition cannot represent.

records.title: An idiv that throws on Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1, where the JVM must return the dividend
records.summary: The interpreter's `idiv` divides on the host and throws on a zero divisor, as the instruction does. A developer adds a second check: `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` is the one quotient an int cannot hold, so report it as an `ArithmeticException` too rather than return the wrong sign. The property the build proves of `idiv`, that dividing by -1 negates on every input, is refuted on exactly that input, with the exception as the outcome: JVMS §6.5 specifies the overflow and forbids the exception.

records.title: A NaN check written as == Float.NaN never fires, and fcmpl quietly becomes fcmpg
records.summary: The interpreter's `fcmp` implements `fcmpg` and `fcmpl` with four branches: less, greater, equal, and the unordered case that the two opcodes decide differently. A developer moves the unordered case to the front, written as `a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN`, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison. The regression proof against the previous version finds an input with a NaN on which `fcmpl` now pushes 1 instead of -1: a comparison with `Float.NaN` is false for every operand, including NaN.

records.title: Switch lowering costs computed in int pick the wrong instruction for wide labels
records.summary: The assembler chooses between `tableswitch` and `lookupswitch` with javac's heuristic: the table's space plus three times its time against the lookup's, computed in `long`. A developer drops the `long`: the costs are a few words and comparisons, and the casts clutter the formula. The regression proof against the previous version finds a label range on which the subtraction `hi - lo` overflows an `int`, and the two versions choose differently.

records.title: tableSizeFor rewritten with numberOfLeadingZeros, proved equal on all 2^32 inputs
records.summary: The symbol table rounds a requested capacity up to a power of two with the five-shift bit smear of JDK 8's `HashMap.tableSizeFor`. A developer replaces the smear with the one-line form JDK 11 adopted, `-1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1)`. The regression proof compiles both versions into one program and proves them equal on every `int`, with the JDK's own bytecode of `numberOfLeadingZeros` in the proof.

records.title: A verifier fast path for "everything is an Object" lets an uninitialized object pass
records.summary: The type checker's assignability relation answers `isAssignable(from, to)` over the verification types, with the uninitialized types assignable to themselves and `top` only. A developer hoists the most frequent answer, that every reference is assignable to `Object`, above the rarer checks. The behavioural contract of the relation, 289 pairs derived from the bytecode, changes in two: `uninitialized` and `uninitializedThis` are now assignable to `Object`, which is the hole a type-checking verifier exists to close.

records.title: Protected access without the receiver rule opens every superclass object to a subclass
records.summary: Access control at resolution time admits a `protected` member from a subclass in another package only through an object of the subclass itself, as JVMS §5.4.4 requires in its "furthermore" clause. A developer drops the clause: a subclass inherits its superclass's protected members, and the receiver's type is the type checker's business. The behavioural contract of the check, 120 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in one: a protected instance member on an arbitrary object of the superclass is now accessible from a subclass in another package.

records.title: Nest-based private access (JEP 181), reviewed as four lines of a 120-line contract
records.summary: Access control admits a `private` member from its declaring class only; nestmates reach each other through the synthetic accessors javac generates. A developer implements JEP 181: a `private` member is also accessible from a class in the same nest. The behavioural contract is regenerated, and its diff is the four cases where the visibility is `private` and the relation is `same nest`, each `false` to `true`. The other 116 cases are proved unchanged, and the diff is what the reviewer approves.

records.title: Looking up StrictMath intrinsics by name on the host gives a pure interpreter reflection
records.summary: The interpreter computes a fixed list of the guest's `StrictMath` functions on the host, by a `switch` on the name. A developer replaces the list with a `MethodHandles.Lookup.findStatic` on the host's `StrictMath`, so that any unary function works without maintaining the list. The capability contract of the module, every capability `none` until now, gains `reflection` at two call sites: the interpreter can now invoke host methods chosen by a string, and the string comes from the guest's constant pool.

records.title: Letting other threads proceed while <clinit> runs hands out a half-built class
records.summary: A thread that needs a class another thread is initializing waits on the initialization lock, as step 2 of JVMS §5.5 says. Class-initialization deadlocks between classes whose initializers refer to each other are a known production problem, and a developer removes the wait: a request during initialization completes normally for every thread, as step 3 already allows for the initializing one. The contract diff is one line and is approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which the second thread uses the class before its initializer has returned.

records.title: One rule for every class-init request waits on its own thread, and TLC finds the deadlock
records.summary: A request for a class being initialized waits, unless it comes from the initializing thread itself, which is a recursive request and completes normally (step 3 of JVMS §5.5). A developer removes the exception: every request during initialization waits, one rule, and the lock serializes everything. The contract diff is one line and is approved. The model checker, with deadlock detection on, finds a five-step run after which no thread can move: the initializer touched its own class, waited for itself, and every other thread waits for it.

records.title: A constant-pool encoder that writes NUL as one byte emits the byte no class file may hold
records.summary: The class-file writer encodes `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` in modified UTF-8, where U+0000 takes two bytes so that no byte of an encoded string is zero. A developer aligns the encoder with standard UTF-8, one byte for every character up to U+007F, and updates the test that said otherwise. The property the build proves of the encoder, that no first byte is zero, is refuted on the one input it can be: the character U+0000, encoded as the byte 0, which JVMS §4.4.7 says no `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` may contain.

records.title: A bisection midpoint written as (low + high) / 2, proved safe for every lookupswitch index
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: The interpreter bisects the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` with the midpoint `(low + high) >>> 1`, the idiom that survived the overflow bug in `Arrays.binarySearch`. A developer writes it as the division it is, `(low + high) / 2`. On every `int` that is the bug; on every index of a `lookupswitch` it is not, because a `Code` attribute holds at most 65535 bytes and a pair takes eight. The property committed for the midpoint carries that bound in its assumption, and the proof goes through; without the bound, the same proof fails in a fraction of a second.

records.title: A lookupswitch bisection rewritten half-open, proved to find every key in a sorted table
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: The interpreter searches the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by bisection, written the classic way: a closed range, two comparisons per step, three exits. A developer rewrites it in the half-open form, one comparison per step and one equality test at the end. The property committed for the search is its specification: on every strictly sorted table, the result is the index of the key when the key is in the table and -1 exactly when it is not, stated with JML's quantifiers over the array. The prover checks the rewritten bytecode against it on every sorted array up to the bound, and the proof goes through in a few seconds.

records.title: An exception table read with an inclusive end_pc hands an exception to the wrong handler
records.summary: The interpreter finds the handler for a thrown exception in the `Code` attribute's exception table: the first entry, in table order, whose range covers the pc of the throwing instruction. The range is `[start_pc, end_pc)`, and the specification itself calls the exclusive end a historical mistake. A developer building a JVM decides not to repeat the mistake and makes the end inclusive, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method. The property the build proves of the lookup, stated over the table's columns as arrays, is refuted, and the counterexample is shrunk to a table of one entry whose `end_pc` is the pc of the throwing instruction, which the patched lookup hands to a handler that does not cover it.

counterexample.expected: result == -1 || (result >= 0 && result < startPc.length && startPc[result] <= pc && pc < endPc[result])

records.title: A constant-pool encoder that writes supplementary characters in four bytes, as UTF-8 does
records.summary: The class-file writer encodes `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` in modified UTF-8, which has two differences from standard UTF-8: U+0000 takes two bytes, and a supplementary character is written as its two surrogates, three bytes each, never in the four-byte form. A developer who knows the second difference as CESU-8, the encoding every other tool deprecates, makes the encoder write the four-byte form for a surrogate pair, with a test for it. The property the build proves of the encoder is the sentence of JVMS §4.4.7 that forbids it: no byte of the encoding is zero, and none lies in `0xf0` to `0xff`. It is refuted on the first array that holds a surrogate pair.

counterexample.expected: result <= out.length && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < result; out[i] != 0 && (out[i] & 0xff) < 0xf0) && (\forall int i; result <= i && i < out.length; out[i] == \old(out[i]))

records.title: A stack map offset loop without the first-frame special case, proved to place every frame
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: A `StackMapTable` frame carries an `offset_delta`, not an offset: the first frame applies at `offset_delta`, every later one at the previous frame's offset plus `offset_delta + 1`. The class file reader's loop says so, with a special case for the first frame. A developer removes the special case by starting the count one byte before the code, so that every frame, the first included, is `offset_delta + 1` past the previous one. The property committed for the reader is the specification's own arithmetic, stated with JML's `\sum`, and a law stated with a call of the reader itself: no two frames share an offset. The prover checks the rewritten loop against both on every table up to the bound.

records.title: A Code attribute length that omits the nested attributes' headers truncates the method
records.summary: The writer of a class file computes the `attribute_length` of a `Code` attribute: twelve fixed bytes, the code, eight per exception table entry, and the nested attributes, each a six-byte header followed by its own `attribute_length` bytes. A developer reads in JVMS §4.7 that an attribute's length does not include its initial six bytes, and makes the loop add each nested attribute's length and nothing else. The property committed for the computation, stated with JML's `\sum` over the nested lengths, is refuted at once; the counterexample JBMC finds is an eight-attribute table of large numbers, which the tool shrinks in its interpreter to one nested attribute of length zero, six bytes short.

counterexample.expected: result == 12 + codeLength + 8 * exceptionTableLength + (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < nestedAttributeLength.length; 6 + nestedAttributeLength[i])

records.title: A constant-pool index that counts the long entry itself points one past the entry
records.summary: Constant pool entries are numbered from 1, and a `CONSTANT_Long` or `CONSTANT_Double` entry takes two numbers, the one after it being unusable: the specification calls this, in retrospect, a poor choice. The class file reader maps an entry's position to its number by walking the entries before it. A developer rewrites the walk as a count of the two-number entries, and counts up to and including the entry itself. The property committed for the mapping, stated with JML's `\num_of`, is refuted on a pool of one long constant, whose number comes out as 2 instead of 1.

counterexample.expected: result == 1 + entry + (\num_of int i; 0 <= i && i < entry; tags[i] == 5 || tags[i] == 6)

records.title: A max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved to find the deepest point
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: The assembler computes `max_stack` for a `Code` attribute: the deepest the operand stack gets, which for a straight-line sequence is the largest running sum of the instructions' stack effects. The loop compares the depth with the maximum after every instruction. A developer compares it only after an instruction that pushes more than it pops, since no other instruction can leave the stack deeper than it was. The property committed for the computation is the definition itself, `\max` over the prefix sums, written as nested JML quantifiers, under the assumption that the effects are those of JVM instructions. The prover checks the changed loop against it on every such sequence up to the bound; stated over every `int` effect instead, the same property refutes the change, on two effects whose sum wraps, which is the premise the developer's argument did not state.

records.title: An idiv that leaves division by zero to the host, proved to throw exactly there
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
records.summary: The interpreter's `idiv` checks for a zero divisor and throws `ArithmeticException` before dividing on the host. A developer notices that the host is itself a JVM, whose division throws the same exception on the same input, and removes the check from `idiv` and `irem`. The property committed for each kernel now declares the exceptional behaviour as JML does, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, instead of assuming the zero divisor away; the prover covers the exceptional path with the normal one and proves that the host throws exactly where the check did.

records.title: An exception table check that rejects a handler range ending at code_length
records.summary: The class file reader checks each exception table entry as JVMS §4.7.3 requires: `start_pc` before `end_pc`, `end_pc` at most `code_length`, `handler_pc` inside the code. A developer makes the three offsets uniform, all of them less than `code_length`, reasoning that an offset into the code is an offset into the code. The property committed for the check is a throws clause, the specification's three conditions as the condition under which the reader throws `ClassFormatError`; the prover refutes the uniform check on the smallest method there is, one byte of code covered by a handler that ends where the code ends, which the patched reader rejects as malformed.

counterexample.expected: a normal return: no throws clause applies to this input
counterexample.actual: throws ClassFormatError("Illegal exception table range in class file")

records.title: An encoder that zero-terminates the string into the caller's buffer
records.summary: `encodeInto` writes the modified UTF-8 encoding of a `char[]` into a buffer the caller provides and returns how many bytes it wrote. A developer adds a zero byte after the encoding when the buffer has room, so that the bytes can be handed to native code as a C string, which is what the encoding's zero-free form exists for. The property committed for the encoder now has a frame condition in JML's `\old`: the bytes past what it wrote are as the call received them. The prover refutes the patched encoder on an empty string and a one-byte buffer, whose byte it zeroes.

counterexample.expected: result <= out.length && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < result; out[i] != 0 && (out[i] & 0xff) < 0xf0) && (\forall int i; result <= i && i < out.length; out[i] == \old(out[i]))

records.title: A lookupswitch pair sort that compares keys by difference
records.summary: The assembler sorts the match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by key, as JVMS §6.5 requires, with an insertion sort that keeps each offset with its key. A developer factors the comparison into a `compare` method that returns the difference of the two keys, the comparator idiom. The property committed for the sort says that the keys come out sorted and that every pair the call received is among the pairs it left, in JML's `\old`. The prover refutes the patched sort on two keys in order whose difference overflows, `Integer.MIN_VALUE + 271` and `272`, which it swaps.

counterexample.expected: (\forall int i; 0 < i && i < keys.length; keys[i - 1] <= keys[i]) && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < keys.length; (\exists int j; 0 <= j && j < keys.length; keys[j] == \old(keys[i]) && offsets[j] == \old(offsets[i])))

records.title: A coordinator that waits for the last vote when every vote so far is yes blocks forever
records.summary: When the vote collection times out, the two-phase-commit coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer makes it keep collecting instead when every vote that did arrive was yes, so as not to throw away a transaction every responder approved. Every safety invariant of the protocol model still holds, and so does the contract diff the reviewer approves. The model's liveness property, that every participant eventually decides, does not: TLC shows a six-step run after which two prepared participants hold their locks forever.

records.title: A grace period for the last vote, proved to keep every participant deciding
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 936 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: The developer of example 057 tries again: when the collection times out with every vote so far yes, the coordinator moves to a new phase, `GRACE`, and waits one more period; a second timeout aborts. The contract gains a phase and seven cases, and the model's guard on the timer, its type invariant and its inductive invariant gain the phase. TLC checks the invariants, the liveness property that every participant eventually decides, and that the protocol still implements Lamport and Gray's transaction commit specification, and all of them hold in every state and every behaviour; and the inductive step holds too, so atomicity is proved for the new protocol by induction, not only by search.

records.title: A server that grants a vote without adopting the candidate's term elects two leaders
records.summary: A Raft server that receives a vote request from a newer term adopts the term and becomes a follower of it, and only then applies the vote rule. A developer stops the adoption, so that a server whose timer fired cannot drag the cluster into a new term by asking: the vote rule already counts a candidate's newer term as a free vote, so the vote is still granted. The contract diff is three cases, one per role, and is approved; the vote rule is untouched and its regression proofs pass. The election model finds a five-step run that ends with two leaders in one term.

records.title: One timeout rule for every role makes a leader campaign against itself
records.summary: A follower or candidate whose election timer fires becomes a candidate of the next term; a leader's timer firing is ignored, since a leader holds no elections. A developer folds the two cases into one: every server runs for office when its timer fires, and the leader's case was dead code because the timer is stopped when a server wins. The contract diff is one case and is approved. Every invariant of the election model holds, because a candidate of term 2 is an ordinary state. The action property that a leader never becomes a candidate does not: TLC shows the four-step run in which a leader deposes itself.

records.title: A leader that steps down when its timer fires, proved to keep one leader per term
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 1,153 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft leader cut off from the majority keeps believing it leads, and keeps serving reads from a state the rest of the cluster has moved past, until some message from the newer term reaches it. A developer adds the check etcd calls CheckQuorum: a leader whose election timer fires, meaning no majority acknowledged it for a whole timeout, steps down to follower. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change keeps every invariant and both action properties, in 1,153 states: one leader per term, terms that never go backwards, and no leader that campaigns.

records.title: A candidate that retries its election without voting for itself again elects two leaders
records.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one: a new term, a vote for itself, a request to every other server. A developer trims the retry: the tally already holds the candidate's own vote, so it need not vote again, and the request goes only to the servers that never answered. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model finds the bug under each of its three safety configurations, each in its own way: a seven-step run of three servers in which two candidates elect each other, the one step that breaks the inductive invariant (a candidate of a term it has not voted in), and an eight-step run of four servers in which a vote cast in term 1 is counted in term 2.

records.title: A candidate that retries in the same term, proved safe, and shown never to elect a leader
records.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one in a new term. A developer makes it ask again in the same term instead, for the votes it lacks, so that a candidate that cannot win does not drive the whole cluster's term up on every timeout. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change safe under three of its configurations: one leader per term, with three servers, by induction, and with four. The fourth configuration, the liveness check, finds the run the safety proofs cannot see: three servers whose timers fire together are three candidates of term 1, each refused by the other two, and under this rule nothing ever starts term 2. The cluster has no leader, for good. A green safety result says exactly what it checked; the liveness property says the rest.

records.title: A candidate that stands down on a timeout, proved safe and live
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 879 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one at once. A developer makes it stand down to follower instead, so that its next timeout, after a full randomized wait, starts the new election: a split vote is then retried by its candidates one at a time rather than all together. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change under all four of its configurations: one leader per term with three servers, by induction, and with four, and under fairness a run that stays within the term budget still elects a leader, and a leader the cluster has left behind still steps down. The liveness check is the one a reviewer wants for a rule that makes candidates stand down: the question is whether the election can stall, and the answer is no, because a follower's timer starts a new term.

records.title: A leader that ignores vote requests from newer terms votes twice in a term
records.summary: A Raft server that hears a newer term from anyone becomes a follower of that term. A developer exempts the leader from the vote request: a leader should keep serving until a newer leader's heartbeat, or a reply from a newer term, proves the cluster has moved on, so that a server that comes back from a partition with an inflated term cannot depose a working leader on every retry. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model finds the bug under all three of its safety configurations: an eight-step run of three servers in which the leader's vote elects two candidates of the same term, the one step that breaks the inductive invariant (a leader that holds a vote cast in an older term), and a longer run of four servers.

records.title: A leader that treats a vote request of its own term as impossible crashes on a split vote
records.summary: The Raft role machine throws on one input, a leader hearing a leader of its own term, because election safety says it cannot happen. A developer extends the reasoning to vote requests: a candidate campaigning in a term that already has a leader is just as impossible, so a leader throws on a vote request of its own term too. The contract diff is one case, from unchanged to an exception, and is approved; the input is covered by a new test, which checks that it throws. The election model has an invariant for exactly this claim, that no input the protocol can deliver makes the role machine throw, and it fails in four steps: two servers time out into term 1, one wins with the third's vote, and the other, still a candidate of term 1, asks the new leader for its vote. A split vote makes the exception reachable, and the leader crashes on the loser's request.

records.title: A coordinator that commits after aborting on timeout, once the late votes are all yes
records.summary: When the vote collection times out, the two-phase-commit coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer adds a second chance: if the missing votes arrive after all and every one of them is yes, the abort was a wrong guess and nothing has been lost, so the coordinator commits. The contract diff is one case, in the `ABORTED` phase, and is approved; the test that said an aborted transaction stays aborted is adjusted to the new rule. The model finds the run the developer did not picture in nine steps, and the inductive step finds it in one: an abort is a decision participants act on, and by the time the late votes are in, a participant that voted yes has aborted on the coordinator's say-so and released its locks. The commit that follows splits the participants.

records.title: A coordinator that answers a late vote with its decision, proved to keep every decision
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 728 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A vote that reaches the coordinator after it has decided comes from a participant that may not have heard the decision, and a prepared participant holds its locks until it does. The developer makes the coordinator answer every late vote by sending its decision again. The contract diff is eight cases, every tally in a decided phase, from unchanged to a transition that stays in the phase and resends. The model proves the change keeps every decision: the same 728 states as before, every invariant and property holding, and the inductive step, which ties what the coordinator broadcasts to the phase it is in, closed under the new rule. Example 067 is the same eight rows done wrong.

records.title: A vote rule that lets a voter switch candidates within a term elects two leaders
records.summary: Raft's vote rule grants one vote per term: a server that has voted for a candidate refuses every other candidate of that term, and a split vote costs the cluster a new term. A developer lets the vote move instead: a candidate still asking in the voter's term is one the term's election has not settled, since the candidate the voter chose has not won, so the vote goes to whoever is asking and the split resolves within the term. The behavioural contract of the vote rule, a second operator of the election model generated from the Java, changes in three rows, and the tests are updated to say so. TLC finds two leaders of one term in five steps: two servers time out together, and each, still a candidate, grants the other its vote. The vote a server cast for itself moves too, and both tallies reach a majority.

records.title: A vote rule without the election restriction elects a leader missing a committed entry
records.verdictLabel: ✗ Violation: LeaderCompleteness, 3-step trace (a server left behind)
records.summary: Raft's vote rule refuses a candidate whose log is behind the voter's, the election restriction, so that a leader never lacks a committed entry. A developer drops it for the approach of Viewstamped Replication, in which the new primary collects the log from a majority after it is chosen: the vote need not wait for the candidate with the best log, since a leader that lacks entries will fetch them before it serves. The contract of the vote rule changes in five rows, and the tests are updated to say so. The election model's four configurations with equal logs verify the change; the fifth, in which one server holds the log a deposed leader left behind, longer than the others' and of an older term, finds in three steps that this server is elected with one vote besides its own, lacking the entry the other two hold and have therefore committed. A Raft leader never collects entries: it makes the followers' logs match its own, and the committed entry would be overwritten.

records.title: A vote rule that compares log length before term grants a vote it must refuse
records.verdictLabel: ✗ Violation: counterexample found to 1 of 3 properties
records.summary: The election model checks the vote rule's decision kernel, generated from its contract, and repeats the arithmetic around it: how the candidate's term and log compare with the voter's own is computed in `grant`, outside the model's reach. A developer reorders that comparison so that the longer log wins and the term of the last entry breaks ties between logs of one length, reading "up to date" as "further along". The kernel's contract does not change and the election model verifies it under every configuration, logs included, since the model does its own comparing. The property that states the election restriction over `grant` itself, that a candidate whose last entry is of an older term is refused however long its log, fails: JBMC shows a voter whose last entry is of a later term granting a candidate whose log is longer but ends in an earlier one, the log a deposed leader left behind. Example 013 catches the same rewrite as a regression against the previous version of the method; this one needs no previous version, only the rule.

counterexample.input: grant(currentTerm=0, votedFor=0, lastLogTerm=0, lastLogIndex=0, candidate=0, candidateTerm=0, candidateLastLogTerm=-1, candidateLastLogIndex=1)

records.title: A vote rule that refuses a repeat request is verified by a model that never asks twice
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified, vacuously: no run takes the 2 rows the change alters
records.summary: Raft's vote rule grants a candidate the vote it already holds: a server votes once per term, and the candidate that has the vote may ask again, because the reply that carried it may have been lost. A developer reads one vote per term literally and refuses the repeat, as a duplicate the tally must not count twice; the contract of the vote rule changes in two rows, and the tests are updated to say so. The election model verifies the change under all five configurations, and for the first time the verdict comes with what it rests on: TLC's coverage of the generated operator, read back row by row by the tool, shows that no run of the model takes either row the change alters. The model's RPCs are atomic, a request and its reply in one step, so no candidate ever asks a voter twice, and the rows for a repeat are dead in it. The verdict is vacuous, and the tool says so.

records.title: A vote rule that throws on a term not adopted, and the model shows the term always is
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 610 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft server adopts a candidate's newer term before it decides the vote, so the vote rule only ever sees a candidate of the current or an older term; its nine rows for a newer term are a courtesy to callers that skip the adoption. A developer makes them throw instead, so that a server which skips the step fails loudly rather than vote in a term it has not entered, and rewrites the tests that relied on the courtesy. The contract changes in nine rows, every one of them to an exception, and the election model verifies the change under all five configurations: its invariant `KernelNeverThrows` asks of every reachable state whether any RPC the state allows would make a kernel throw, and none does, because the role machine adopts the candidate's term in the same step, before the vote rule is asked. Coverage shows the nine rows taken by no run, which for rows that throw is the point, and the tool does not call the verdict vacuous: a row that throws is meant never to be taken, and whether no run can take it is what the invariant checked.

records.title: A follower that leads on a late majority passes a model that never counts votes late
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified, vacuously: no run takes the 1 row the change alters
records.summary: Raft's role machine ignores a tally counted by a server that is no longer a candidate: the votes are of an election the server has left. A developer lets a follower that finds a majority in its tally take the leadership, reasoning that a candidate which stepped down while its votes were in flight was elected all the same; the contract changes in one row the model can see, and a test says so. The election model verifies the change under all five configurations, and coverage shows that no run takes the row: in the model a vote is counted in the step that grants it, by the candidate itself, and a server that steps down in that step empties its tally first, so there is no late majority to count. The verdict is vacuous, and the tool says so. In a cluster the late votes are of the term the server left: a candidate of term 1 that heard the leader of term 2, stepped down, and then counted its term-1 majority would lead term 2 beside its leader.

records.title: An open breaker that restarts its wait on each refused call never probes under load
records.summary: An open circuit breaker refuses calls until its wait has passed, then lets a probe through. A developer makes each refused call start the wait over, so that a caller which keeps hammering a failing dependency holds the breaker open until it stops; the contract changes in one row, from a rejection to a transition that stays open and starts the wait, and the test of the open state is updated to say so. Every safety invariant of the model holds: an open breaker still lets nothing through before its wait, still shields the dependency, still probes a limited number of times. The liveness check, a second configuration of the same model under fairness conditions, finds the run in which the caller never stops: two failures open the breaker, the dependency comes back, and from then on every tick of the clock is answered by a call that starts the wait over. The breaker stays open forever over a dependency that has recovered.

records.title: A half-open breaker that judges its probes as a window is proved safe and live
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 98 states, and under 1 more configuration
records.summary: A half-open circuit breaker used to reopen on the first probe that failed. A developer makes it judge the probes together once the last has completed, as Resilience4j does: a failed probe is recorded like any other outcome, and the failure rate of the probes decides between closing and reopening. The contract changes in three rows, the test that expected the first failure to reopen is rewritten, and the model verifies the change under both configurations: every safety invariant in every state, and every liveness property under fairness, the three that say an open breaker probes again, a dependency that comes back is used again, and a dependency that stays down gets its wait between rounds of probes. The verdict comes with what it rests on: runs of the model take one of the three rows the change alters, a failed probe before the window is complete with the failure rate at the threshold, and the other two, a failed probe with the rate below the threshold, are rows the model's two probes and threshold of one in two can never produce.

records.title: A half-open breaker that starts over on a failed probe keeps probing a dead dependency
records.summary: A half-open circuit breaker reopens on a probe that fails, and the wait starts again. A developer makes a failed probe start the probes over instead, so that one bad probe does not condemn a dependency on its way back and the breaker closes on the permitted number of successes in a row; the contract changes in four rows, from reopening to a half-open state with its metrics reset, and the test of a failed probe is updated to say so. Every safety invariant holds. The liveness check finds the run in which the dependency stays down: the breaker opens, waits, probes, and from the first failed probe on it is half-open forever, probing a dead dependency at the rate of its probe cap, with no wait ever again. The property that fails is the one that says a dependency which stays down gets the wait between its rounds of probes.

records.title: An in-progress record that expires by age lets a retry run beside the first attempt
records.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver's sweeper releases a key once its record's time to live has passed, but only a completed record: a record in progress never expires. Support still reports clients stuck in 409 loops after a worker died mid-request, and a developer makes the sweeper release records in progress too, on the reasoning that a record in progress for a whole time to live belongs to a worker that is gone. The contract diff is one row, and the model checker has never exercised it: the model's record did not expire. Under a second configuration in which it can, TLC finds a six-step run in which the record expires under a worker that is alive, and the client's retry executes beside it.

records.title: An expired key kept as a tombstone refuses late retries, proved at most once
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 168 states, and under 1 more configuration
records.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver releases a key when its record's time to live passes, so a retry that arrives after that is a new request and executes again. The developer makes the record expire in two steps instead: the response goes and the key stays as a tombstone that refuses a late retry, then the tombstone goes too. A new key state, a new effect, six new or changed rows in the contract, and a model whose type invariant has to learn the state. TLC checks every interleaving of three attempts under both configurations of the model, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, with the coverage saying which of the new rows the runs exercised.

records.title: Dropping an expired response but keeping its key replays a response that is gone
records.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver releases a key when its record's time to live passes, and a retry after that executes the request again. A developer wants both the storage back and the guarantee kept: when the time to live passes, drop the stored response, which is the bulk of the record, and keep the key, so that a late retry is recognised and never run twice. The contract diff is one row and a new effect; the tests pass. Under the configuration in which the record expires, TLC finds a seven-step run in which the late retry is recognised, and answered with a response that no longer exists.

records.title: A role machine that adopts the term of a stale reply sends a term backwards
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine adopts the term of a reply to one of its own RPCs when that term is newer than its own, and otherwise leaves its role alone. A developer rewrites the rule as a switch over the reply's term, with the arm for the current term written out and every other term adopted, on the reasoning that a reply whose term differs from the server's own is a reply from a server out of step with it, and the term in the reply is the one to be in. The contract diff is three rows, one per role, for a reply from an older term, and the model checker had never taken any of them: an RPC in the model was one step, so a reply always carried the server's own term or a newer one. Under a sixth configuration in which a vote reply waits on the wire, TLC finds a five-step run in which a candidate that has moved on to term 2 takes the reply of term 1 and goes back to it, which the action property that terms never decrease reports.

records.title: A role machine that treats a stale reply as impossible crashes on a late reply
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine leaves its role alone on a reply from the current term or an older one. A developer makes a reply from an older term throw `IllegalStateException`, the exception the kernel already reserves for an input it holds impossible, on the reasoning that a server answers with the term it has now and the asking server's term only grows while it waits, so a reply cannot carry a term older than the server's own. That reasoning is the model's own simplification written into the Java: an RPC in the model was one step, so no run had ever handed the role machine such a reply, and the three rows that now throw had never been taken. Under the sixth configuration, in which a vote reply waits on the wire, the invariant that no reachable state lets the kernel throw fails in four steps: a candidate asks for a vote, times out into the next term, and the reply of the old term is waiting for it.

records.title: Logging of stale replies, verified by the configuration that delivers them
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 610 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine leaves its role alone on a reply from the current term or an older one. A developer tuning election timeouts wants to know how often replies arrive after the server has left the term they answer, and makes the role machine return a `LOG_STALE_REPLY` effect on a reply from an older term, with the role unchanged. The contract diff is three rows, one per role, each from unchanged to a transition to the same role with the one effect. Under the five configurations the model had, no step takes any of the three rows, and the verdict would have been verified vacuously; under the sixth, in which a vote reply waits on the wire, every run takes them, and every invariant and action property holds in 20,351 states. The change is verified by the configuration that delivers the replies it is about.

records.title: A candidate that stands down for a rival of its term votes twice in it
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine leaves its role alone on a vote request from its own term; the vote rule refuses it, since the candidate has voted for itself. To cut split votes short, a developer makes a candidate that hears a rival of its own term stand down for it, as a follower of the term, so that the rival gets its vote. The contract diff is one row, and under the six configurations the model had, every invariant and action property holds: the server that stands down also drops its own tally, so no run elects two leaders. The paper's rule is that a server votes for at most one candidate per term, and the server that stood down has voted twice in the one term, for itself and for the rival; a seventh configuration, in which a history variable records every vote cast, reports it in four steps. The rule is what the paper's argument for election safety rests on, and the change breaks the argument whether or not this kernel goes on to break the conclusion.

records.title: A leader that yields to a candidate of its own term lets the term elect twice
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine leaves its role alone on a vote request from its own term, so a leader that hears a candidate of its term goes on leading; the candidate is a server its heartbeats did not reach, and it will lose, since the majority voted for the leader. A developer makes the leader step aside instead, as a follower of the term, so that the election the candidate is holding can finish. The contract diff is one row, and under the six configurations the model had, every invariant and action property holds: the leader that yields is a follower before the candidate wins, so no state has two leaders of one term, and the invariant that a leader holds a majority is true of each in turn. The paper's election safety property is about the run, at most one leader can be elected in a given term, and a seventh configuration, in which a history variable records every term a server has led, finds the run that elects two in five steps: the leader's own vote, forgotten when it yielded, is the one the candidate wins with.

records.title: A leader that answers a candidate of its term with heartbeats, proved its only leader
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 610 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft server's role machine leaves its role alone on a vote request from its own term, so a leader that hears a candidate of its term goes on leading and waits for its next heartbeat to make the candidate step down. A developer has the leader send its heartbeats at once instead: the row for a leader and a current-term request returns a transition to `LEADER` with `SEND_HEARTBEATS`, where it returned unchanged. A transition where there was an unchanged decision is a change in kind, on the row that example 085 turned into a step-down, and the reviewer wants to know that it keeps the role, adopts no term and frees no vote. Under all seven configurations every invariant and property holds, the two that are about the whole run included, at most one leader elected per term and one vote per server per term; the coverage shows the changed row taken under all seven configurations.

records.title: A coordinator that aborts the transaction on restart reverses a commit it had sent
records.summary: A two-phase-commit coordinator logs each phase change before it acts on it, and a restart after a crash reads the log: a logged decision is sent again, since the crash may have come before the broadcast, and no logged decision means abort. A developer collapses the three cases of the recovery rule into one, abort: whatever the coordinator was doing, an abort releases the participants' locks, and a transaction that was about to commit can be retried. The contract diff is one row, a restart in `COMMITTED`, from sending the commit again to aborting. The two-phase-commit model is now checked under two more configurations, in which the coordinator may crash between steps or between logging a decision and sending it, and restarts on the recovery rule, generated from the contract like the decision rule. Under the two the model had, nothing crashes and the row is never taken. Under the third, TLC finds in ten steps a commit that is sent, applied by one participant, and then reversed by the restarted coordinator, which tells the other two to abort; the fourth finds the same step from a state its inductive invariant admits.

records.title: A coordinator with nothing to redo on restart leaves a logged decision unsent forever
records.summary: A restarted two-phase-commit coordinator sends a logged decision again, because the crash may have come between logging it and sending it. A developer sees only duplicate broadcasts come of it, since the coordinator cannot tell whether the first copy went out and so always sends a second, and makes a restart in a decided phase change nothing, as the decision rule does for any event in a decided phase. The contract diff is two rows, and the change mirrors the rule beside it. Under the two configurations the model had, nothing crashes and the rows are never taken; the inductive invariant is closed under the new rule as well, since every state the run passes through is one it admits. The third configuration, in which the coordinator may crash twice, finds the run in eight steps: two participants vote yes, the coordinator crashes as it counts the first of them, the third participant gives up, and the coordinator restarts, logs the abort that presumed abort calls for, and crashes again before sending it; the second restart finds a logged abort and the new rule has nothing to redo. The two prepared participants hold their locks forever, a liveness failure, reported as a run that stays in its last state. The fourth configuration finds the step that makes it possible, a coordinator up and decided with nothing out.

records.title: A coordinator that resumes collecting votes on restart, proved safe and live
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 728 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A restarted two-phase-commit coordinator without a logged decision aborts: presumed abort, the rule for a coordinator that cannot tell what it had counted. This coordinator logs its tally with each vote, so a developer has a restart in `COLLECTING` carry on instead, counting the votes still on their way and aborting on the timer if the rest never come, so that a crash no longer costs a transaction whose votes were all yes. The contract diff is one row. The model proves the change keeps the protocol safe and live under all seven configurations: the two without crashes as before, and with crashes, every invariant in every reachable state, every participant deciding under the fairness conditions, every behaviour one transaction commit allows, and the inductive step closed under the new restart, with the changed row taken in both configurations that have a crash.

records.title: A coordinator node that broadcasts before it logs, caught by its own recorded run
records.summary: The two-phase-commit coordinator node logs each phase change before it broadcasts the decision, so that a crash between the two loses the broadcast and the restart sends it again. A developer swaps the two to take the log write off the participants' wait. The decision rules are untouched, every contract holds, and the model's six configurations are as green as before: the model never sees the glue. The seventh configuration does. TLC walks the runs the nodes recorded and finds, four steps into the one in which the timer's abort is logged and the coordinator crashes, a step the model has no action for: the decision is out and the log still says collecting. In the run that commits, the restart then presumes abort after a commit has gone out.

records.title: A coordinator node that logs the tally only with a decision forgets the votes in a crash
records.summary: The coordinator node writes its log on every vote it counts, so that the tally survives a crash, which is what the model assumes of it. A developer cuts the writes down to one per decision: a vote that decides nothing is kept in memory. No rule changes, every contract holds, the tests pass, and the model's six configurations are green. The trace check finds, four steps into the run in which the coordinator crashes while collecting, a step the model has no action for: the crash takes the counted vote with it, where the model's `Crash` keeps the tally. The model's verdicts about restarts no longer describe this coordinator.

records.title: A participant that votes no when it gives up, its recorded runs all steps of the model
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 637 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A participant that gives up before voting aborts in silence, and the coordinator finds out when its timer fires. A developer has the participant's rule vote no as it gives up, so that the coordinator can abort on the vote, and reworks the scenario that covers it: the coordinator now receives the no and aborts once every vote is in, with no timer. The contract's row gains the effect, the model's `ParticipantTimeout` carries it out, and TLC checks the rule under all seven configurations: the invariants, the liveness property and the refinement hold with and without crashes, the inductive step holds, and the recorded runs are all steps of the model. The state counts of the explored configurations drop, since giving up now leaves the states a no vote does.

records.title: A restarted participant that releases its locks aborts what the coordinator committed
records.summary: A two-phase-commit participant that voted yes holds its locks until it hears the decision, through a crash and a restart: it cannot decide alone, which is the blocking property of the protocol. A developer has a restarted participant release its locks and abort, so that a crash does not leave the data locked while the coordinator is slow; the coordinator's timer, the comment says, covers the rest. The contract gains the row, the tests pass, and the model's first four configurations are as green as before, since no participant crashes in them. The sixth, in which they do, finds in eight steps a transaction the coordinator commits on three yes votes and a participant that voted yes, crashed in the same step, and restarts aborted. The inductive step with participant crashes refuses the restart too.

records.title: A participant node that sends its vote before logging it restarts as if it had not voted
records.summary: The participant node logs its new state before it sends its vote, so that a crash between the two loses the vote and not the state, and a restart that reads `PREPARED` holds the locks. A developer swaps the two to get the vote to the coordinator sooner. The rule is untouched, every contract holds, and the model's six configurations are as green as before: the model says the participant logs first, and nothing in it checks that the node does. The recorded runs do. TLC walks the run in which a participant crashes after its first I/O operation and finds, at its second step, a state the model has no action for: the yes vote is on its way and the log still says working. A restart from that log aborts, and the vote can still reach the coordinator.

records.title: A restarted participant that votes no rather than wait for the timer, proved safe and live
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 728 states, and under 6 more configurations
records.summary: A participant that crashes before voting restarts aborted, since no vote of its went out, and says nothing: the coordinator finds out when its timer fires. A developer has the restarted participant vote no as it aborts, so that the coordinator can abort on the vote rather than on its timer. The contract's row gains the effect, the model's `ParticipantRecover` carries it out, and TLC checks the rule under all seven configurations: the invariants, the liveness property and the refinement of transaction commit hold with the participants crashing, the inductive step holds with the new row among the steps, and the recorded runs, one scenario reworked to deliver the restarted participant's no, are all steps of the model.

records.title: A follower that takes entries after a conflicting previous entry breaks log matching
records.summary: A Raft follower refuses a leader's entries unless it holds the entry before them, the consistency check of section 5.3, so that the leader backs up one entry at a time until the logs agree. A developer relaxes the check to the previous index existing, whatever entry is there: the leader's later entries overwrite the conflict in due course, the comment says, and a round trip is saved. The tests pass and the contract diff is eight rows. The replication model's first configuration, three servers, three terms and two entries, finds in twelve steps two logs that hold the same entry of term 3 at index 2 over different entries at index 1, which is what the log matching property forbids and what the check exists to prevent; the second, figure 8 of the paper, finds a follower that applies an entry nobody else committed, and the third, three terms and one entry under fairness, the same.

records.title: A leader that commits an earlier term's entry by counting replicas loses it to a rival
records.summary: A Raft leader marks an entry of its own term committed once a majority of the servers hold it, and an entry from an earlier term only along with one of its own after it, the rule of section 5.4.2. A developer has the leader commit any entry a majority holds, whatever its term, with the argument that a candidate without such an entry cannot win a majority. The tests pass, the contract diff is one row, and the model's first configuration, three terms, verifies the change in 25,666 states, and so does the third, under fairness. The second, four terms and one entry per leader, the budget of figure 8 of the paper, finds in sixteen steps a leader of term 3 that commits an entry of term 1 while a rival whose log ends in term 2 has just been elected leader of term 4 without it.

records.title: A follower that drops a conflicting previous entry at once, proved safe
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 19,844 states, and under 3 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft follower that holds an entry of another term at the index before the entries a leader sends refuses the request and keeps the entry: the leader backs up, sends from one entry earlier, and the conflicting entry is replaced then. A developer has the follower drop the conflicting entry and everything after it the moment it refuses, so that the leader's next try finds the index free. The contract's eight rows change from a rejection to a transition that truncates, the model's `Replicate` carries the truncation out and backs the leader up as before, and TLC checks the rule under all three configurations: log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety hold in 19,844, 8,578 and 14,244 states, no committed entry is ever overwritten, the followers still catch up and learn every commit under fairness, and six of the eight changed rows are taken, the two left being for an entry the follower already holds, which a one-step RPC never sends.

records.title: A follower that leaves its commit index alone on a heartbeat never applies the last entry
records.summary: A Raft follower moves its commit index up to the leader's on every request it accepts, a heartbeat included, as far as its log is known to match the leader's. A developer makes a heartbeat a liveness signal and nothing more: the commit index moves with the entries, the comment says, and a request that carries nothing to apply changes nothing. The tests pass and both safety configurations verify the change: no committed entry is overwritten, the logs match, and a follower never applies what the leader has not. The replication model's fairness configuration reports a run that goes on forever after eight steps: the leader replicates its entry to both followers, marks it committed, and every heartbeat from then on is refused the commit index it carries, so the followers never apply it; the property that every follower learns the leader's commits is violated, and the run ends in a state the system never leaves.

records.title: A follower that refuses to overwrite a conflicting entry never catches up
records.summary: A Raft follower that holds an entry of another term at the index a leader sends an entry for drops it, and everything after it, and takes the leader's. A developer has the follower refuse such a request instead, so that no entry is discarded on a leader's say-so, with the leader backing up as it does on a conflict at the previous index. The tests pass, and the two safety configurations verify the change: a follower that refuses changes nothing, and nothing it holds breaks an invariant.
