The fairness configuration reports a run that goes on forever after eleven steps: the leader is already at the start of the follower's log, has nothing to back up to, sends the same entry again and is refused again, and the follower never holds the leader's log; the property that every entry in a leader's log reaches every follower is violated, and the run ends in a state the system never leaves.

records.title: A follower that takes the commit index on the heartbeat after an entry, proved live
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 21,551 states, and under 3 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft follower that appends an entry takes the leader's commit index in the same request, as far as the entries it now holds. A developer has it take the commit index only on a request that appends nothing, the heartbeat that follows, once the entry is on disk: a request that appends is a write, and the commit index moves on the next one. The change is verified under all three configurations, the two safety ones in 21,551 and 9,269 states, and the fairness one in 14,958: every entry still reaches every follower, every follower still learns the leader's commits, a leader's own entries are still committed, and the coverage shows both rows the change alters taken under each.

records.title: A leader that moves a follower up on a refusal records entries the follower lacks
records.summary: A Raft leader keeps, per follower, the index of the next entry to send and the last index it knows the follower's log to match its own: an accepted request moves both up, a refused one backs the next index up by one, and the commit rule counts the servers whose match index reaches an entry. A developer has every reply move the follower up, with the argument that whether the follower took the entries is the append rule's business and the next request compares the logs again. The tests pass and the contract diff is one row. The replication model's first configuration finds the consequence in twelve steps: s1, leader of term 1, appends an entry and replicates it to s2; s2 times out, wins term 2 with s1's vote and appends an entry of its own; it sends s3, whose log is empty, the new entry after the old one, which s3 refuses, lacking the old one, and the patched rule records s3 as holding both; s1 times out and wins term 3 with s3's vote, s3's log being empty; and s2, which has not heard of term 3, counts itself and s3 as a majority for its entry and marks both committed. Leader completeness is violated: the leader of term 3 lacks an entry the leader of term 2 has committed, and will overwrite it with its own.

records.title: A leader that backs up on a refusal it has moved on from sends the follower what it holds
records.summary: A Raft leader backs a follower's next index up by one when the follower refuses the request at it, and ignores a refusal it has already moved on from: a reply that arrives late, or arrives twice, about a request the follower has since accepted. A developer has every refusal back the follower up, with the argument that the follower lacked the entry when it answered and a round trip more is the most it can cost. The tests pass, the contract diff is one row, and the three configurations in which an RPC is one step verify the change: the rule is never handed a refusal it has moved on from, which TLC's coverage says. The replication model's fourth configuration, in which a reply waits on the wire and may be handed to the leader twice, finds the consequence in twelve steps: a leader of term 2 holding one entry sends a follower without it a heartbeat, which the follower refuses, backs up, sends the entry, which the follower takes, and then is handed the refusal again; it backs up again, below the entry it has just recorded the follower as holding, and from there sends that entry forever, since each acceptance of it tells the leader nothing its record does not hold. The invariant that the next index is past the match index is violated.

records.title: A leader that takes a late acceptance as news moves a follower back, proved safe
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 20,253 states, and under 3 more configurations
records.summary: A Raft leader ignores an acceptance of entries it has already recorded the follower as holding: a late or repeated reply moves nothing backwards. A developer has the leader take the follower's word whenever it comes, late or not: an acceptance says what the follower held when it answered, the record follows it, and the next request carries what the follower has already, which it accepts again. The tests pass, the contract diff is one row, and the change is verified under all four configurations, the three in which an RPC is one step and the one in which a reply waits on the wire and may be handed to the leader twice, which is the one in which the changed row does anything: a leader with an empty log whose heartbeat a follower accepts, which then appends an entry and replicates it, and is handed the heartbeat's acceptance again, records the follower as holding nothing and sends the entry again, which the follower accepts a second time. The record says less than the follower holds, never more, and the commit rule, which counts the record, counts fewer servers than hold the entry, never more.

records.title: apache/commons-numbers#223: ArithmeticUtils.pow accepts (-2)^31, found and confined from bytecode
records.verdictLabel: ✗ the intended change found; ✓ confined to it; ✓ Javadoc proved
records.summary: A pull request that lets `ArithmeticUtils.pow(int, int)` return `Integer.MIN_VALUE` for `(-2)^31` instead of throwing. The regression proof found the one changed input, `pow(-2, 31)`, from the two versions' bytecode in 185 s; the Javadoc was proved on the new version; and the change was proved confined to that input on all 2^64 others in 18 minutes.

records.title: apache/commons-lang#1750: ArrayUtils.reverse with Integer.MIN_VALUE as the end index
records.verdictLabel: ✗ the bug's input found; ✓ change confined; ✓ new version never throws
records.summary: A pull request that stops `ArrayUtils.reverse(array, start, end)` wrapping an end index of `Integer.MIN_VALUE` to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. The bug's input was found for all six primitive overloads and shrunk to an empty array; the change was proved confined to that end index on arrays of up to four; the new version was proved to throw on no input.

records.title: apache/commons-lang#1585: ArrayUtils.subarray index arithmetic overflow
records.verdictLabel: ✗ the overflow found; ✓ change confined; ⚠ length property unverifiable
records.summary: A pull request that clamps `ArrayUtils.subarray`'s end index from below, because `end - start` could overflow to a positive size. The overflow was found: the old version runs out of memory where the new returns an empty array. The change was proved confined to the inputs where the subtraction overflows; a length property is unverifiable because JBMC treats an array of computed size as one of any length.

records.title: FasterXML/jackson-core#1203: division by 1000 as multiply-and-shift, nothing proved
records.verdictLabel: ⚠ unverifiable: solver budget; one precondition witness
records.summary: A pull request that replaces `number / 1000` with `(int) (number * 274_877_907L >>> 38)` in `NumberOutput`. Nothing was proved: each proof pits a 64-bit multiplication against a 32-bit division, and the solver did not finish in its budget or ran out of memory. One witness documents the precondition, `number >= 0`.

records.title: apache/commons-codec 43a9aa66: Hex decoding restricted to ASCII, after modelling the JDK
records.verdictLabel: ✓ new version proved; ⚠ old version needs a model of Character.digit
records.summary: A maintainer's commit that makes `Hex.toDigit` accept only ASCII hexadecimal digits, so that Unicode digits cannot bypass textual blocklists. Two false violations were traced to JDK classes JBMC has no model of and fixed with a forked charset models library and cache models; the new `toDigit` then proved in full, while the old one needs a model of `Character.digit`.

records.title: An Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders drops the request body's validation on the way
records.summary: Clients already send an `Idempotency-Key` on `POST /concerts/{id}/holds`, so a developer makes `POST /orders` accept the same header, writing the handler's new parameter list by hand. The `@Valid` on the request body does not survive the edit. Every test passes: they post well-formed orders. The module's boundary contract, the routes and the advice on each read from the compiled classes, shows the `POST /orders` line changing from a validated body to an unvalidated one, next to the header that was added.

counterexample.actual: POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@RequestHeader(name = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String idempotencyKey, @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)

records.title: A PaymentVoided event joins the sealed PaymentEvent family without its @JsonSubTypes entry
records.summary: The payment service voids an order whose refund arrives before any charge, and until now told nobody. A developer adds a `PaymentVoided` record to the sealed `PaymentEvent` interface, publishes it on the void path, and handles it in ticketing, where the compiler insists on the new case of the sealed switch. The `@JsonSubTypes` list on the interface, which names the type id of each event on the wire, is not touched. Every test passes: the compiler checked the Java side, the codec test round-trips the three events it knew about. Jackson writes the new event with the type id `PaymentEvent$PaymentVoided` and the consumer rejects it. The regenerated boundary contract of the `contracts` module shows the new type with a `!` line saying exactly that.

counterexample.actual: ! PaymentVoided is a permitted subtype that @JsonSubTypes does not list: it is written under the type id "PaymentEvent$PaymentVoided", which a reader of PaymentEvent rejects

records.title: A prod profile raises the hold seat limit under boxoffice.hold.max-seat, a key nothing reads
records.summary: Production wants a hold to be able to take a whole row, so a profile document for `prod` is added to the ticketing service's `application.yaml` with `boxoffice.hold.max-seat: 12`. The key the code reads is `max-seats`. Spring Boot ignores a key nothing binds, so production keeps the default of 8, and no test runs with the `prod` profile. The module's boundary contract lists each configuration key with the value each profile gives it and who reads it; the regenerated contract has a new line for the mistyped key, with a `!` under it that names the nearest known key.

records.title: A nested Billing record on PlaceOrder carries @NotBlank constraints that no @Valid leads into
records.summary: Orders gain billing details for the receipt: a nested `Billing` record with `@NotBlank` and `@Email` on its fields, added to `PlaceOrder` as a `@NotNull` component. The handler validates the request with `@Valid`, so the author expects a blank name or a bad email to be refused. Bean Validation does not step into a nested object unless the property itself carries `@Valid`, so the only check that runs on the billing details is that they are present; every test posts valid ones and passes. The module's boundary contract lists each wire type with its constraints, and the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the new property saying that the constraints on `Billing` are not checked.

records.title: A @Cacheable on the concert lookup with no @EnableCaching in scope: every call still reads Mongo
records.summary: A concert does not change after it is created, and every hold and order reads it, so the developer puts `@Cacheable("concerts")` on the store's lookup. The annotation compiles, the context starts, every test passes, and nothing is cached: no configuration in the ticketing service's scope carries `@EnableCaching`, and Spring Boot does not switch caching on by itself. The module's boundary contract has an activation block that names, for each kind of annotation the module uses, what enables it; the regenerated contract has a new line `@Cacheable: nothing enables it` with a `!` line under it.

records.title: HoldDocument.idempotencyKey renamed, the query strings not: a retried POST holds the seats twice
records.summary: The developer renames `HoldDocument.idempotencyKey` to `requestKey`; the IDE renames the component and its javadoc, the hold is built positionally, so nothing else changes and everything compiles. The mapper now stores the key under `requestKey`, while `TicketingStore.holdByIdempotencyKey` still runs `where("idempotencyKey")` and the unique index is still on `idempotencyKey`: the lookup matches nothing, the index covers nothing, and a client that retries `POST /concerts/{id}/holds` with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets a second hold on other seats. The boundary contract's stored types block shows the document's shape and checks every field-name string in the module against it; the regenerated contract has three new `!` lines under `HoldDocument`.

counterexample.actual: ! TicketingStore(MongoTemplate) indexes "idempotencyKey": not a field of HoldDocument, OrderDocument or SeatDocument, so the index is on a field that is never set

records.title: GET /holds/{id} now extends the hold it returns: a polling checkout page keeps seats held for ever
records.summary: The developer makes `GET /holds/{id}` keep the hold alive: `HoldService.get` pushes the expiry of the hold and of its seats forward on every call, so a customer filling in the payment form does not lose the seats under them. The checkout page polls that endpoint for its countdown, so a hold now never expires while a tab is open, a browser's prefetch or a monitor's probe keeps seats off the market, and a retried GET changes state. The boundary contract now says what each entry point reaches (the documents it reads and writes, the topics it sends to, the HTTP calls it makes, the events it publishes); the regenerated contract has `writes HoldDocument, SeatDocument` under the GET and a `!` line: a safe method with side effects.

records.title: Payment command sent to Kafka from inside the order transaction: the outbox dropped for a dual write
records.summary: The developer drops the outbox from the order path: `OrderService.place` sends the `ChargePayment` command to Kafka itself, from inside the MongoDB transaction that records the order, so the payment service hears about the order at once instead of on the relay's next poll. The send is not part of the transaction. A write conflict makes `Transactions.run` retry the work, and each attempt sends a fresh command with a fresh id; a transaction that rolls back after the send has told the payment service to charge for an order that does not exist; a process that dies between the commit and the send leaves an order that waits for a payment nobody was asked for. The boundary contract places every effect with respect to transactions; the regenerated contract has `sends payments.commands` under `POST /orders` and a `!` line: a transaction that sends.

records.title: Hold route variable renamed in the template but not in the parameter: a 500 on every request of it
records.summary: The developer renames the path variable of `GET /holds/{id}` to `{holdId}`, so the route reads like the OpenAPI description, and leaves the handler's parameter as `@PathVariable String id`. Spring binds a `@PathVariable` by name, the annotation's or the parameter's, at request time: no template of the route has a variable named `id`, so every request of the route ends in `MissingPathVariableException`, a 500. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now checks each handler's request binding; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the renamed route: `@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}`.

records.title: HoldExpiredException replaces the ConflictException and no handler maps it: a 500 instead of a 409
records.summary: The developer gives the expired-hold case of `POST /orders` its own exception, `HoldExpiredException`, carrying the hold id, so that callers and logs can tell it from the other conflicts, and leaves `ApiErrors`, the `@RestControllerAdvice`, as it was. The new class extends `RuntimeException`, not `ConflictException`, so no `@ExceptionHandler` takes it and no `@ResponseStatus` marks it: a client that places an order for an expired hold now gets a 500 from the container's error page instead of the 409 problem detail. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now lists under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under `POST /orders`: `throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500`.

counterexample.actual: POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request): ! throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500

records.title: A Retry-After rewritten around two unchanged refill helpers, proved equal in a second
records.summary: The wait a refused request is told to make is rewritten from `credited + period - now` to `period - (now - credited)`, around the two refill helpers it calls and leaves alone. Each helper holds a 64-bit division, and relating two copies of each across the versions is more than the solver settles in a minute. The proof takes the unchanged helpers as one function in both versions, never sees their arithmetic, and is done in a second.

records.title: A tie-break reordered to group its parameters by kind, proved equal under the stated reordering
records.summary: The last-writer-wins tie-break took its two writes interleaved, `(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)`; a developer groups the parameters by kind, timestamps first, and writes the body as the comparison chain the javadoc describes. A regression proof needs the same signature in both versions, and this one changed. The developer states the relation instead, `winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)` from the new parameters, and the proof is of the new method against the previous one called that way, on every input.

records.title: A cache expiry in milliseconds left expires entries in their last millisecond, found by the relation
records.summary: The same rewrite as example 123, the expire-after-write boolean turned into the time an entry has left, but in milliseconds, as the cache's metrics report it; callers test `<= 0`. The developer states the relation to the previous version, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof finds an entry with a fraction of a millisecond to go: not expired before, no millisecond left now, so expired. The integer division rounds the last fraction of a millisecond down to none.

records.title: A cache expiry turned from a boolean into the time left, proved expired exactly when none is left
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: A cache's expire-after-write test returned whether an entry had expired. A developer turns it into the time the entry has left, so that an eviction can be scheduled for the moment it expires and the metrics endpoint can report it, and callers test `<= 0`. A regression proof compares results of one type, and these are a boolean and a long. The developer states how they are related instead, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof is of that relation between the new method and the previous one on every input the cache can pass.

records.title: A partitioner rewritten with floorMod keeps every hash on a partition and moves every negative key
records.summary: Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its bit mask, is rewritten as `Math.floorMod(hash, n)`, which also lands every hash on a partition: the module's property still holds and the tests pass. The regression proof, run by the tool's own checker, finds that every negative hash now goes to a different partition than before. Half the keys of a topic move on deploy, and the records of such a key straddle two partitions.

records.title: A JWT skew moved from the window's ends to the clock, proved equal by the tool's own checker
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: The clock-skew tolerance of a JWT validator is moved from the token's window, `now >= nbf - skew && now < exp + skew`, to the clock, `now + skew >= nbf && now - skew < exp`. Within the module's precondition the two are the same arithmetic, and the tool's own checker proves it in a fraction of a second, with no JBMC; outside it they differ where a sum of seconds overflows a `long`, which the checker also shows when run without the scope.

records.title: A backoff's doubling loop replaced by a shift overflows, found on the record's components
records.summary: The exponential backoff is a record, `Backoff(baseMillis, capMillis)`, and the delay before an attempt is its method: the base doubled by a loop that stops at the cap. The loop is replaced by `Math.min(capMillis, baseMillis << attempt)`, and the tests pass. The regression proof, which now takes a method of a record and builds the receiver from symbolic components, finds the shift leaving the range of a `long`: a wait of `Long.MIN_VALUE` milliseconds, which a scheduler runs at once, so a failing dependency is retried without pause.

records.title: A backoff's doubling loop replaced by a shift kept short of overflow, proved equal on the record
records.summary: The same rewrite as example 126, done right: the delay is `baseMillis << attempt` with the shift distance kept below the leading zeros of the base, so that a shift that would leave the range of a `long` is replaced by one that is already past the cap, and a non-positive attempt returns the base. The regression proof on the record's components shows the closed form equal to the loop for every base, cap and attempt the constructor admits, in six seconds.

records.title: A batch commit made the batch record's method loses the check on the failed index
records.summary: The offset a batch listener commits after a batch was a static function of the batch's start, its size and the index of the record that failed. The start and the size become a record, `Batch(start, size)`, with the function as its method and the guard on the batch in the record's compact constructor; the part of the guard about the failed index, which is no component, goes with it, and the tests pass. The regression proof, which relates the record's method to the static function called with the components, finds an index past the batch committing past it: records the listener never processed are never read again.

counterexample.input: offsetToCommit(this=Batch[start=0, size=1], failedIndex=1), previously offsetToCommit(batchStart=0, batchSize=1, failedIndex=1)
counterexample.expected: throws IllegalArgumentException("batchStart >= 0, batchSize > 0 and -1 <= failedIndex < batchSize are required")

records.title: A batch commit made the batch record's method, proved equal on the batch's components
records.summary: The same refactor as example 128, the batch's start and size gathered into a record `Batch(start, size)` with the commit arithmetic as its method and the guard on the batch in its compact constructor, with the check on the failed index kept in the method, since the index is no component. The regression proof relates the record's method to the static function called with the components and proves them equal on every batch the constructor accepts and every index, in half a second.

records.title: A backoff that gained a multiplier counts a negative attempt down to the cap
records.summary: Crosscut's `Backoff` record, the retry filter's wait between attempts, gains a `multiplier` component (Spring Retry's `ExponentialBackOffPolicy` has one, 2 by default) and the doubling loop is rewritten around it, counting the attempt down to zero instead of up to it. An attempt below zero, which the old loop treated as zero and answered with the base, now counts down past zero and multiplies until the cap. The tests pass, none of them passing a negative attempt. The regression proof relates the new record to the old one by building the old `Backoff` from the new components, `new Backoff(this.baseMillis, this.capMillis)`, with the multiplier of two as the scope of what should not have changed, and finds the attempt of minus one in nine seconds.

counterexample.input: delayMillis(this=Backoff[baseMillis=1, capMillis=2, multiplier=2], attempt=-1), previously delayMillis(this=Backoff[baseMillis=1, capMillis=2], attempt=-1)

records.title: A backoff that gained a multiplier proved equal to the doubling record for a multiplier of two
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: The same change as example 130, done right: the `multiplier` component is added, the loop keeps counting up and multiplies by it, and the cap is applied once after the loop instead of in every turn. The regression proof relates the three-component record to the two-component one by building the old `Backoff` from the new base and cap, and shows the delay unchanged for every base, cap and attempt when the multiplier is two, the scope of what the change was not meant to touch.

records.title: A refill that counts periods from the epoch credits a token for a nanosecond
records.summary: A token bucket's refill, `(nowNanos - lastNanos) / periodNanos` whole periods, is rewritten as `nowNanos / periodNanos - lastNanos / periodNanos`, so that two clock readings are never subtracted. The tests pass, every refill in them starting at time zero, and the module's property holds. The regression proof, run by the tool's own checker within the module's precondition, finds a refill one nanosecond into a period that credits a whole token: a client that polls at each period boundary earns two tokens a period, and the limiter admits twice its rate.

records.title: A refill capped by the room left proved equal to the capped sum within the module's precondition
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: A token bucket's refill, `Math.min(capacity, tokens + earned)`, is rewritten as `tokens + Math.min(earned, capacity - tokens)`, the tokens earned but no more than the bucket has room for, so that the sum can never overflow. Within the module's precondition the two are the same arithmetic, and the tool's own checker proves it in half a second, with no JBMC; outside it they differ where a sum overflows a `long`, which the checker also shows when run without the scope.

records.title: A window counter that advances by one window leaves its start behind a quiet client
records.summary: Crosscut's `Window` record, the fixed-window request counter a rate-limiting filter keeps per client, gains a `previousCount` component for the sliding-window estimate (Cloudflare's approximation: the previous window's count weighted by how much of it the sliding window still covers). The counting method is rewritten with it: a request in the same window adds one, and a request after it opens the next window, carrying this window's count. The tests pass, polling one window after another. But a client quiet for two or more windows gets a window starting one window after its old one, behind the clock, with the count of a window long gone carried into the estimate: its next request opens yet another window, so the count never passes one and the limit never applies to it. The regression proof relates the new record result to the old one on the components they share, `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`, with the old counter built from the new components, and finds a request two windows ahead.

counterexample.input: counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0, previousCount=0], nowNanos=2, windowNanos=1), previously counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0], nowNanos=2, windowNanos=1)

records.title: A window counter with the previous count proved equal on the start and the count
records.summary: The same change to Crosscut's `Window` record done right: the counter gains a `previousCount` component and an `estimated` method, and `counted` keeps the alignment of the start to the clock, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`, carrying the count only into the window right after the one it was in. The regression proof relates the new record result to the old one on the two components they share, with the old counter built from the new components, and proves the start and the count equal on every input, the tool's own checker in seconds.

records.title: A window start aligned by masking opens a window per request unless the window is a power of two
records.summary: Crosscut's `Window` record, the fixed-window request counter a rate-limiting filter keeps per client, aligns a window's start to the clock with a remainder, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. A rewrite clears the reading's low bits instead, `nowNanos & -windowNanos`, which is the same alignment when the window is a power of two, and the tests are changed to one (`1L << 30`, about a second). The filter is configured in seconds: with a window of a billion nanoseconds the mask is not the alignment, every request lands in a window of its own, and the count never passes one, so no client is ever refused. The regression proof finds it on the smallest window that is not a power of two, in a fraction of a second with either engine, and proves the rewrite unchanged where the window is a power of two when that is stated as the scope.

records.title: A window start aligned by a mask on power-of-two windows and by the remainder elsewhere proved equal
records.summary: The same rewrite of Crosscut's `Window` counter done right: a window that is a power of two aligns its start by clearing the reading's low bits, `nowNanos & -windowNanos`, the fast path for the filter's default windows, and any other window by the remainder as before. The regression proof shows the counter unchanged on every counter, reading and window: the tool's own checker in 0.5 s, the division left to the solver under the facts of every division, among them that a power of two divides by masking; JBMC did not finish the same harness within a minute.

records.title: A window start computed as the window's index times its length proved equal to the remainder form
records.summary: Crosscut's `Window` counter computes the start of the window a reading falls in as `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. A rewrite names the window's index first, `nowNanos / windowNanos`, and multiplies it back: the form a reader expects, and the one that gives the index a name for a log line or a key. The two are equal by Java's division identity, `d == (d / p) * p + d % p` for every `d` and `p`, which no engine proved within a minute until the tool's own checker learned it: a quotient times its divisor is now the dividend less the remainder, the same bits the old version computes, and the proof over every counter, reading and window takes 0.1 s.

records.title: A window index held in an int refuses every request after two billion windows
records.summary: The same rewrite of Crosscut's `Window` counter as example 138, the start computed as the window's index times its length, with the index held in an `int`: `(int) (nowNanos / windowNanos)`. Two billion windows into the clock's range the cast wraps, the start comes out negative, and the record's constructor refuses it: every request from then on throws out of the rate limiter. The regression proof finds it in 3 s, on a window of one nanosecond at a reading of 2^31, a case no test with a sensible window reaches.

counterexample.actual: throws IllegalArgumentException("the start and the count must not be negative")

records.title: A half-open bisection that answers the empty table first throws for a key above the last match
records.summary: The interpreter searches the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by bisection, written the classic way: a closed range, two comparisons per step, three exits. A developer rewrites it in the half-open form, one comparison per step and one equality test after the loop, and, since an empty table has no midpoint, answers the empty table first and drops the guard on the final test. For a key above the last match the loop leaves `low` at the table's length, and the final test reads past the end: the instruction throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of taking the default branch. The tests pass, because their table ends in `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, which no key is above. The regression proof, run by the tool's own checker over the symbolic table, finds `find(matches=[0], key=1)` in a fraction of a second: -1 before, the exception after.

counterexample.actual: throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException("Index 1 out of bounds for length 1")

records.title: A lookupswitch bisection rewritten half-open proved equal to the closed form on every sorted table
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: The same rewrite of the interpreter's `lookupswitch` bisection as example 140 done right: the half-open range `[low, high)`, one comparison per step, and the final equality test guarded by `low < matches.length`. The regression proof relates the new search to the old one on every strictly sorted table of up to eight matches and every key, the sortedness stated as the scope with a quantifier over the array, and the tool's own checker proves it in two seconds where JBMC's one formula over the symbolic table takes a hundred. Without the scope the two searches differ, on an unsorted table where they probe different midpoints, which the checker shows in a tenth of a second.

records.title: An ASCII fast path for the constant-pool encoder proved equal to the previous version at bound eight
records.summary: The class-file writer encodes every string constant into modified UTF-8 with `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto`, which tests each `char` for the one-, two- or three-byte form. Most constants are ASCII, so a developer adds a fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters, recognised by `(char) (c - 1) < 0x7f`, is copied without the general test, and the general loop takes over at the first character that is not. The regression proof against the previous version, which JBMC could not finish at the default bound of eight characters in 2.8 GB, is done by the tool's own checker in 7 s and 76 MB: once the search has grown past a few hundred paths, the paths through the loops are merged at their join points, so the proof explores 733 paths where there are 11643, and at a bound of twelve characters it is done in 83 s where the unmerged search exhausted its budget of 200000 paths without a verdict.

records.title: An ASCII fast path that admits U+0080 writes it in one byte, which the properties allow
records.summary: The class-file writer's `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto` gains an ASCII fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters is copied without the general test. The test is written `(char) (c - 1) <= 0x7f`, which admits U+0080 along with U+0001 to U+007F, and writes it as the single byte `0x80`, where modified UTF-8 needs two: a class file with such a constant is rejected by the virtual machine. The encoder's committed properties, about how many bytes each character takes and what its first byte is, hold of the leading run too, since they are checked on the general loop's inputs; only the comparison with the previous version catches it. The tool's own checker refutes the proof in 1.1 s and 60 MB on `encodeInto(chars=['\u0080'], out=[32])`, with the paths past the first few hundred merged at their join points, where JBMC ran out of memory at the default bound.

counterexample.expected: throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException("Index 1 out of bounds for length 1"), leaving out=[-62]

records.title: A short-table scan declared as the intended change, whose proof covers no table at the default bound
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified, vacuously: no input in the domain reaches the calls
records.summary: The interpreter's `lookupswitch` search gains a linear scan for tables of at most eight pairs, and the regression proof is asked to show the bisection unchanged on the rest: `--unchanged-unless 'matches.length <= 8'`. The default bound on array parameters is eight, so every table in the domain is among the intended inputs, the harness returns before calling either version, and the proof covers no input. The verdict is verified, vacuously, and the tool says so on a line of its own, found by running the statement with the calls replaced by the assertion's failure.

records.title: The bound raised past the scan limit: the bisection proved unchanged on the tables the scope admits
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
records.summary: Example 144's declaration with the bound on array parameters raised to twelve: the domain now holds tables of nine to twelve pairs, which the scope `matches.length <= 8` admits to the proof, and the tool's own checker proves the bisection unchanged on every such table and every key in 4 s. The vacuity line is gone, since the probe finds a table that reaches the calls. The proof is of the branch the change did not touch, which is what the declaration asked; the notes carry the proof of the scan itself.

records.title: A timeout rule folded as dead code in a refactor is checked as built
records.summary: The change of example 060, made as a refactor: a developer folds the leader's case of the election timeout into the follower's and candidate's, calls the leader's case dead code, and does not regenerate the role machine's contract, since nothing is meant to change. The tests pass. The election model is generated from the role machine's contract, and a runner that generated it from the committed contract unless a behaviour change was intended would check the old rule, and pass whatever the patch did. The runner derives the contract from the patched classes on every run instead: one case differs from the committed contract, which nobody approved, and the model, checked on the rule that was built, shows the leader deposing itself in four steps.

records.title: A contract that says Random.nextInt never throws is refuted on the JVM before the proof relies on it
records.summary: Crosscut's retry filter gains full jitter: a wait drawn by `Random.nextInt` below a ceiling the base doubled by a shift kept short of the sign bit with `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`. The tool's own checker implements none of the three JDK calls, so under `--gaps advised` the agent driving it writes a contract for each. Its contract for `nextInt` says the call returns a value in [0, bound) and nothing else, which is true wherever this kernel calls it. The tool tests every contract on a real JVM before it relies on one: the JDK's `nextInt` throws `IllegalArgumentException` at `bound=0`, the contract is refused with the JVM's counterexamples, its gap stays open, and the proof stops there, with the other two contracts accepted.

records.title: Full jitter proved below the cap on an agent's contracts, one proved against the JDK and two tested
records.summary: The jitter of example 147, with the agent's contract for `Random.nextInt` corrected to say that it throws `IllegalArgumentException` when the bound is not positive. The proof by the tool's own checker reaches three JDK calls it does not implement and closes on the agent's contracts for them alone: the one for `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros` is proved against the JDK's own bytecode of `java.lang.Integer`, the two for `java.util.Random` are tested on a real JVM. On those, a wait is never negative and always below the cap, on every input, and an invalid policy is refused, and the verdict says which contracts it rests on and how each was checked.

records.title: Full jitter proved on the contract library's contracts alone, checked once and not again by the run
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input, relying on 2 contracts for gaps (2 tested)
records.summary: The jitter of examples 147 and 148, proved with no contract of the agent's at all. The proof by the tool's own checker reaches two JDK calls it does not implement, `new Random(long)` and `Random.nextInt(int)`, and the tool's contract library closes each: its contracts for them were tested once on a real JVM, and the run applies them on the record of that check without checking them again. Under `--max-trust 0`, the policy CI uses, the proof may rest on no unchecked contract, and it rests on none.

records.title: A retry throttle rewritten with min and max proved equal on every throttle its constructor makes
records.summary: Crosscut's retry throttle (gRPC's retry throttling: a failure takes a token, a success gives back the token ratio, retries only while more than half the tokens are left) is a mutable object every call on a channel shares. `recorded` is rewritten in the form gRPC's Java client uses, one clamp with `Math.max` and `Math.min` and the threshold doubled instead of halved. The regression proof takes the throttle as an object made by its constructor from symbolic limits, compares the result and the throttle's fields as both versions leave them, and proves them equal on every input, the claim saying that its throttles are the ones the constructor makes: full ones.

records.title: A throttle kept across a config update turned into a copy loses the failures of the calls in flight
records.summary: When a channel's service config is updated with the same retry limits, `reconfigured` hands back the channel's throttle itself, so the calls in flight, which hold it, keep counting their failures into the throttle the channel goes on using. The change hands back a copy with the same tokens and the same limits instead: every field agrees when it returns, and a failure recorded afterwards by a call in flight goes into the old object, which nothing reads, so a failing backend gets retries the throttle would have refused. The regression proof observes the identity relations within each version and refutes the change with `result == throttle`, which holds before and not after; the witness is a construction recipe, replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM.

counterexample.expected: Throttle{limits=ThrottleLimits{maxTokens=1, tokenRatioMilli=1}, milliTokens=1000}, with result == throttle and result.limits == throttle.limits

records.title: A throttle that drops its floor at zero is proved only on full throttles, where it cannot differ
records.summary: The same rewrite of `recorded` as 150, but the floor at zero tokens is gone: `Math.min(next, ceiling)` without the `Math.max(0, …)`. A failure on a drained throttle now takes it below zero, and every token below zero is ten more successes (at a ratio of 0.1) before the channel may retry again: after three failures on a two-token throttle it takes 21 successes instead of 11. The regression proof verifies the change, because its throttles are made by their constructor, which makes them full, and one failure never drains a full throttle; the verdict says `on every input of constructor-made objects` and the domain names the constructor, so the result is a claim about full throttles only, not a proof that the rewrite is right.

records.title: A refill helper rewritten as whole periods, proved once and one function in its caller's proof
records.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter`, the time up to which a refill has credited the bucket, is rewritten from `now - (now - last) % period` to `last + (now - last) / period * period`, the whole periods counted and added back. Its caller, the `Retry-After` of a refused request, is unchanged. Run with the proof cache, the regression proof of the caller first proves the helper's two versions equal on every input, as a check of its own, and stores that proof. It then takes the helper as one function in both versions of the caller, whose statement names the helper's proof by its claim key. Where example 120 shares a helper because its bytecode is identical, this one shares a helper that changed, on the strength of its own proof.

records.title: A refill helper aligned to the clock's grid, refuted alone, and its caller sends a client back early
records.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter` is rewritten to credit the bucket up to the start of the period the clock reading falls in, `now - now % period`, as the fixed window aligns its start. A bucket's periods are counted from its last refill, not from the clock's zero, so the credited time moves whenever the last refill is off the clock's grid. Run with the proof cache, the proof first checks the helper on its own and refutes it, so the helper stays as written in both versions. The caller's proof, the `Retry-After` of a refused request, then finds a client told to wait 1 ns where the old code said 2, which comes back and is refused again. The tests pass, and so does the caller's property that the wait is never more than a period.

records.title: A retry route and its policy refactored, proved to send what they sent, in order, on every input
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: the trace of boundary calls, the response and the outcome preserved on every input
records.summary: A webhook dispatcher's failure route and the Crosscut retry policy behind it are both rewritten: the policy as one expression over two helpers, the route around the policy's answer with each Kafka send in a method of its own. The tool proves, for every status, idempotency and attempt count, that the route answers the same status and attempts the same sends, to the same topics with the same payloads in the same order, as before.

records.title: A retry route that skips the dead letter for a client error loses the delivery without a trace
records.summary: The same refactor of the failure route and its retry policy, with one shortcut added: a 4xx other than 408 and 429 answers 200 at once, since no retry fixes it. The answer is the same as before and every test passes, but the delivery is no longer dead-lettered. The effect check finds a request on which the old route sends a dead letter and the new one sends nothing, and replays it on a JVM.

records.title: A retry route that dead-letters a delivery out of attempts sends the dead letter twice
records.summary: The same refactor of the failure route and its retry policy, with the case of a delivery out of attempts handled first: it is dead-lettered whatever the receiver answered, and the route then goes on to ask the policy, which refuses, and dead-letters it again. The answer is the same and every test passes; the effect check finds the duplicate send, in exact order, and replays it on a JVM.

records.title: A quote's amount made a value object, proved at its route and in its kernel with no mapping written
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: preserved on every input of the stated domain, with nothing written by hand

The tool compares the two builds whole: the route `POST /quotes` answers the same total and sends the same event on every request, and the kernel's `total` and `withQuantity` do what they did under a relation between the old and new quotes that it inferred itself; the rewritten helper is proved once and used as one function in `total`'s proof, and a rerun is an exact hit of every proof.

records.title: A cent too much per item, refuted at the route and in the kernel, no inferred mapping absorbing it

The input mapping `old.cents == new.amount.cents + 1` would make the totals agree, is not vacuous and is even a bijection, and it would hide the regression; the tool never proposes it. The route and the kernel's `total` are both refuted on one cent for one item, each witness replayed on the JVM.

records.title: A quote handed back as a copy with the same values, refuted on identity alone

Every field agrees with what 190 hands back; a caller that keeps the quote it passed and the one it got back sees two objects where it saw one. The tool holds the method to `result == q` within each version and refutes it on that alone, the witness replayed on the JVM with the objects' identities.

counterexample.expected: Quote{cents=0, quantity=0}, leaving q=Quote{cents=0, quantity=0}, with result == q

records.title: A bulk order's quote event dropped in the refactor, refuted on the route's trace of sends
records.summary: The value-object refactor of 190, with the route sending no `QuoteEvent` for an order of 100 items or more. The total is the same on every request, so every test of the answer passes. The tool compares the ordered trace of the route's sends and refutes it on a 100-item order, the witness replayed on the JVM under recording stubs.

records.title: A bulk order's quote event sent twice, refuted on the route's trace in exact order
records.summary: The value-object refactor of 190, with the route sending the `QuoteEvent` a second time for an order of ten items or more. The answer is the same, and so is the last event sent, which is what a test of a producer usually checks. The tool compares the whole ordered trace of sends and refutes it on a ten-item order, the witness replayed on the JVM under recording stubs.

records.title: A total wrong only for a quote no constructor makes, proved only on the quotes the constructor makes
records.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: preserved on every input of the stated domain, with nothing written by hand
records.summary: The value-object refactor of 190, with `total` returning a wrong amount for a quantity of zero or less, which `Quote`'s constructor refuses. The tool proves `total` preserved, and its result says over what: quotes made by their constructor, from any arguments it accepts. The bug is outside that claim, and the claim says it is.

records.title: A route renamed in the refactor, left unresolved with a question for each observation it carried
records.summary: The value-object refactor of 190, with `POST /quotes` renamed to `POST /quote`. records.title: spring-boot@e8de5a6d: the Outcome enum keeps WebMvcTags.outcome's tags (positive scaffold)
records.summary: Boot's 2019 change that moves HTTP outcome classification into an `Outcome` enum and rewrites `WebMvcTags.outcome(HttpServletResponse)` to `Outcome.forStatus(status).asTag()`. The positive of the metric-label family: both revisions should give the same tag key and value for a null response and every int status, and each revision's tag takes one of six values. A partial scaffold: source-locked, claims frozen, oracle, driver, probes and mutant written; not yet built or run through the pipeline.

records.title: spring-framework@db9a10bf: simpleMatch's prefix check as startsWith (positive scaffold)
records.summary: Framework's 2021 change of one expression in `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch(String,String)`, from `pattern.substring(0, i).equals(str.substring(0, i))` to `pattern.startsWith(str.substring(0, i))`. The positive of the binder decision-string family: both revisions should return the same boolean and exceptions over a bounded UTF-16 domain. Maven Central's spring-core 5.3.6 and 5.3.7 carry exactly the parent's and child's source. A scaffold: source-locked, tasks named, not yet run.

records.title: spring-security@fe9e4549: BCrypt.hashpw with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 (positive scaffold)
records.summary: Security's 2019 change of `BCrypt.hashpw(String,String)` from `password.getBytes("UTF-8")` with an AssertionError wrapper to `password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`. The positive of the password-bytes family: on fixed salts from upstream's tests and a frozen password domain (null, malformed surrogates and invalid salts included), both revisions should return the same hash or exception class.
